title: Identify and maintain the types of records required in own industry and understand why it is necessary to create evidence and maintain confidentiality

lessons.title: Why we keep records
lessons.html:
Records are proof

A record is information written down or saved on a computer that shows what happened, when it happened and who did it. In the wool and mohair industry, and on farms, records are needed every day. Without records, nobody can prove how many bales arrived, how much a bale weighed, or which worker took a sample.

Records are used to

  • pay farmers correctly for their fibre;
  • trace a bale or sample from arrival to sale;
  • pay workers correctly;
  • show that safety rules and procedures were followed;
  • answer complaints and claims from buyers;
  • show auditors and inspectors that the business follows the law and standards;
  • plan work and make decisions.

Records as evidence

If something goes wrong, records are the evidence of what really happened. For example, a buyer says a bale was missing. The signed delivery note, with the bale count and the driver's signature, shows whether all bales were loaded. If there is no record, the store may have to pay the claim.

A record is only good evidence if it is:

  • accurate – the facts are correct;
  • complete – nothing is left out;
  • made at the time – written when the work is done, not days later from memory;
  • signed and dated – so we know who made it and when;
  • readable – clear writing or typing.

lessons.title: Types of records in our industry
lessons.html:
The records you will see

RecordWhat it shows
Delivery notes and waybillsWhat was received or sent, and who signed
Farmer specificationsBales sent by each farmer, with marks and descriptions
Receiving registerDate, farmer, bale numbers and condition on arrival
Weight listsMass of every bale
Sample registersSamples taken, by whom and when, and where they were sent
Store location recordsWhere every lot is in the store
Dispatch recordsBales sent, buyer, truck, container and seal numbers
Time sheets and leave formsHours worked and leave taken
Injury and incident registerAccidents and near misses
Machine checks and maintenanceForklift, press and scale checks; scale calibration
Training recordsWho is trained and licensed for which machine

Paper and computer records

Some records are on paper, some on the computer, and some on both. Paper records are filed in the right file, in order. Computer records are saved in the right folder or system and backed up.

How long to keep records

Records must be kept for the time the company and the law require. Do not throw away or delete records unless your supervisor tells you it is allowed.

Who uses these records?

Many people depend on the records you keep. The office uses weight lists to pay farmers. Buyers use test results and dispatch records. Managers use time sheets to pay wages. Auditors check training and machine records. A mistake in one record can affect all these people.

lessons.title: Keeping records correct and confidential
lessons.html:
Look after the records

Filling in records

  • Write in pen, clearly.
  • Fill in every space. Write "n/a" if something does not apply.
  • Check numbers twice.
  • Sign and date.
  • If you make a mistake, draw one line through it so it can still be read, write the correct value and initial it. Never use correction fluid or tear out pages.
  • Never change someone else's record or sign for someone else. This is dishonest and can be fraud.

Confidentiality

Some information is private. Confidential means it may only be seen by people who need it for their work. Examples:

  • workers' personal details, wages, medical and disciplinary records;
  • farmers' names, addresses, bank details and how much they were paid;
  • prices and buyer information.

The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) protects people's personal information in South Africa. Businesses must keep it safe and use it only for the right purpose.

How to keep information confidential

  • Do not talk about private information with friends, family or other workers.
  • Lock files away and lock the computer when you leave.
  • Do not share your password.
  • Do not leave papers on desks or copiers.
  • Shred or dispose of old private papers as the company says.

Key points

  • Records show what happened, when and who did it, and are used as evidence.
  • Good records are accurate, complete, made at the time, signed, dated and readable.
  • Correct mistakes with one line and initials; never use correction fluid or sign for others.
  • Keep records for the time the company and law require.
  • Personal and business information is confidential; POPIA protects personal information.
